checks.title: Is the EKS cluster API server endpoint configured with private access enabled?
checks.evidence: endpointPrivateAccess=true
checks.recommendation: Enable the private API endpoint (endpointPrivateAccess=true) so in-VPC clients and nodes do not leave the VPC.

checks.title: Is public API server access restricted to specific CIDR ranges rather than reachable from the whole internet?
checks.evidence: endpointPublicAccess=true with publicAccessCidrs [0.0.0.0/0]: the API server is reachable from the whole internet
checks.recommendation: Restrict publicAccessCidrs to known operator ranges, or turn the public endpoint off.

checks.title: Do you allow users to assume an IAM Role and map that role to a Kubernetes RBAC group, rather than creating individual user mappings in the aws-auth ConfigMap?
checks.evidence: governance question: process only, not assessed from cluster data; confirm with the team
checks.recommendation: Map IAM roles (not users) to Kubernetes groups, through access entries where possible.

checks.title: Do you use a dedicated IAM role to create EKS clusters that is not used for routine cluster operations or day-to-day management tasks?
checks.evidence: governance question: process only, not assessed from cluster data; confirm with the team
checks.recommendation: Create clusters with a dedicated role that is not used for daily operations.

checks.title: Is pod-level workload identity (EKS Pod Identity or IRSA) configured for workloads that need AWS access?
checks.evidence: 3/3 workload service accounts whose pods call AWS have a Pod Identity association or an IRSA role
checks.source_file: posture/serviceaccounts.json, posture/cluster.json, posture/oidcproviders.json, posture/podidentity.json, posture/nodes.json, posture/daemonsets.json, posture/pods.json
checks.recommendation: Give workloads that call AWS their own role with EKS Pod Identity or IRSA instead of the node role.

checks.title: Do you restrict access to the kube-system namespace to super administrators only, preventing regular users from modifying critical cluster components?
checks.evidence: governance question: process only, not assessed from cluster data; confirm with the team
checks.recommendation: Limit write access to kube-system to cluster administrators.

checks.title: Do non-system ClusterRoles avoid wildcard (star) resource and verb permissions?
checks.evidence: 0/4 non-system ClusterRoles use a wildcard verb or resource
checks.recommendation: Replace wildcard verbs and resources in custom ClusterRoles with the specific ones needed.

checks.title: Is cluster access granted through EKS access entries (API authentication mode) rather than the legacy aws-auth ConfigMap?
checks.evidence: authenticationMode API_AND_CONFIG_MAP: the aws-auth ConfigMap is still read
checks.recommendation: Move authenticationMode to API and grant access through EKS access entries.

checks.title: Is an OIDC provider configured for the EKS cluster to enable IRSA?
checks.evidence: an IAM OIDC provider matches the cluster issuer
checks.recommendation: Register the IAM OIDC provider for the cluster issuer before relying on IRSA.

checks.title: Is cluster-admin restricted to the two built-in subjects expected to hold it?
checks.evidence: cluster-admin bound only to Group system:masters and User eks:addon-manager; no system:masters mapping in aws-auth
checks.recommendation: Remove cluster-admin bindings other than Group system:masters and User eks:addon-manager, and any system:masters mapping in aws-auth.

checks.title: Do service accounts use namespace-scoped permissions (not cluster-wide)?
checks.evidence: 5/5 workload service accounts are bound only by namespaced RoleBindings
checks.recommendation: Bind workload service accounts with namespaced RoleBindings instead of ClusterRoleBindings.

checks.title: Are role bindings free of stale references to non-existent subjects?
checks.evidence: every RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding subject exists
checks.recommendation: Remove role binding subjects that no longer exist.

checks.title: Do default service accounts in non-system namespaces have automountServiceAccountToken disabled?
checks.evidence: 1/4 default service accounts in workload namespaces set automountServiceAccountToken false
checks.recommendation: Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on each namespace default service account.

checks.title: Is an external secrets manager operator (e.g. External Secrets Operator) deployed on the cluster?
checks.evidence: no External Secrets Operator or Secrets Store CSI Driver found
checks.recommendation: Consider an external secrets operator so application credentials live in a managed store.

checks.title: Do you leverage AWS Secrets Manager and Config Provider (ASCP), EKS secrets encryption, or third-party solutions like HashiCorp Vault to manage secrets in EKS?
checks.evidence: governance question: process only, not assessed from cluster data; confirm with the team
checks.recommendation: Keep application credentials in AWS Secrets Manager (ASCP or an external secrets operator) rather than in manifests.

checks.title: Do you implement automatic rotation of secrets, credentials, and TLS certificates?
checks.evidence: governance question: process only, not assessed from cluster data; confirm with the team
checks.recommendation: Rotate credentials and TLS certificates automatically.

checks.title: Do you implement automatic rotation of secrets, credentials, database passwords, and TLS certificates used by your EKS workloads, using tools like AWS Secrets Manager, External Secrets Operator, or cert-manager?
checks.evidence: governance question: process only, not assessed from cluster data; confirm with the team
checks.recommendation: Automate rotation for workload credentials, database passwords and certificates.

checks.title: Are EBS volumes used by the cluster encrypted at rest?
checks.evidence: 12/12 EBS volumes attached to node instances are encrypted
checks.recommendation: Encrypt the EBS volumes this cluster uses (enable EBS encryption by default for the account and Region).

checks.title: Is the cluster configured to envelope-encrypt Kubernetes Secrets with a customer-managed KMS key?
checks.evidence: encryptionConfig provider keyArn is a customer managed KMS key
checks.recommendation: Configure envelope encryption of Kubernetes Secrets with a customer-managed KMS key.

checks.title: Do you enable encryption at rest for Amazon EFS file systems used by Pods?
checks.evidence: governance question: process only, not assessed from cluster data; confirm with the team
checks.recommendation: Create EFS file systems used by pods with encryption at rest.

checks.title: Are StorageClasses configured with encryption enabled for new volumes?
checks.evidence: 1/1 StorageClasses set encrypted: true
checks.recommendation: Set encrypted: "true" on every EBS StorageClass.

checks.title: Do you enable encryption in transit for Amazon EFS when using the EFS CSI driver?
checks.evidence: governance question: process only, not assessed from cluster data; confirm with the team
checks.recommendation: Mount EFS with encryption in transit (the EFS CSI driver tls mount option).

checks.title: Is a service mesh control plane (Istio, Linkerd or Consul) deployed?
checks.evidence: no service mesh control plane found
checks.recommendation: Where zero-trust service-to-service traffic is required, deploy a service mesh control plane.

checks.title: Do workload pods carry a service-mesh sidecar (the data path for service-to-service mTLS)?
checks.evidence: 0/8 workload pods carry a mesh sidecar
checks.recommendation: Inject mesh sidecars into workload pods where mTLS between services is required.

checks.title: Are Ingress resources configured with TLS termination?
checks.evidence: 2/2 Ingress resources set tls
checks.recommendation: Terminate TLS on every Ingress (spec.tls, or an ALB certificate-arn with an HTTPS listener).

checks.title: Are Kubernetes Network Policies deployed to control Pod-to-Pod traffic?
checks.evidence: network policy enforcement on (aws-node aws-eks-nodeagent --enable-network-policy=true); 4/4 workload namespaces have a NetworkPolicy
checks.source_file: posture/networkpolicies.json, posture/namespaces.json, posture/daemonsets.json, posture/pods.json, posture/vpccniconfig.json, posture/nodeclasses.json, posture/nodes.json
checks.recommendation: Turn on NetworkPolicy enforcement (VPC CNI network policy agent, or the Auto Mode Network Policy Controller) and add policies to every workload namespace.

checks.title: Do you apply network separation to Pod networking using Kubernetes Network Policies or AWS security groups to control traffic between Pods and clusters?
checks.evidence: governance question: process only, not assessed from cluster data; confirm with the team
checks.recommendation: Separate pod traffic with NetworkPolicies or security groups for pods.

checks.title: Is inbound SSH (port 22) closed to the internet on the cluster security groups?
checks.evidence: no cluster security group rule opens port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0
checks.recommendation: Remove inbound port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0; use SSM Session Manager for node access.

checks.title: Do security groups follow least-privilege (no 0.0.0.0/0 on non-standard ports)?
checks.evidence: no 0.0.0.0/0 rule on a non-standard port in the cluster security groups
checks.recommendation: Remove world-open inbound rules outside TCP 80/443 from cluster and node security groups.

checks.title: Do ECR repositories have scan-on-push enabled?
checks.evidence: repository scan settings are judged at registry level (SEC-POSTURE-62)
checks.recommendation: Scan the images this cluster pulls; configure registry-level scanning (see SEC-POSTURE-62).

checks.title: Do ECR repositories use immutable image tags?
checks.evidence: 1/3 ECR repositories use immutable tags
checks.recommendation: Set image tag mutability to IMMUTABLE on the repositories this cluster pulls from.

checks.title: Has the cluster security group's default allow-all egress been narrowed?
checks.evidence: the cluster security group keeps its default allow-all egress
checks.recommendation: Narrow the cluster security group egress from all traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 to what the cluster needs.

checks.title: Is any non-AWS validating admission webhook deployed whose rules match Pod creation?
checks.evidence: no non-AWS validating admission webhook matches Pod creation
checks.recommendation: Run a validating admission webhook (policy engine) that inspects pod creation.

checks.title: Are Pod Security Standards labels applied to namespaces to enforce security baselines?
checks.evidence: 3/4 workload namespaces carry pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce baseline or restricted; failing: legacy
checks.recommendation: Label every workload namespace pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline or restricted.

checks.title: Is a policy engine (Kyverno or Gatekeeper) deployed with at least one policy loaded?
checks.evidence: no Kyverno or Gatekeeper found
checks.recommendation: Deploy a policy engine (Kyverno or Gatekeeper) with enforcing policies loaded.

checks.title: Are admission controller policies (Gatekeeper/Kyverno) deployed on the cluster?
checks.evidence: no Kyverno or Gatekeeper found
checks.recommendation: Load admission policies covering the baseline Pod Security controls.

checks.title: Is an admission policy engine deployed with at least one policy loaded, which is where a privileged-container restriction would live (whether any loaded policy restricts privileged is reported, not scored)?
checks.evidence: no Kyverno or Gatekeeper found
checks.recommendation: Load an enforcing policy that rejects privileged containers.

checks.title: Is an admission policy engine deployed with at least one policy loaded?
checks.evidence: no Kyverno or Gatekeeper found
checks.recommendation: Run admission policies in enforce mode once audit results are clean.

checks.title: Are workload container images pinned to a digest or an explicit tag rather than :latest?
checks.evidence: 14/14 workload containers name a digest or an explicit tag other than latest
checks.recommendation: Pin workload images to a digest or an explicit version tag, never :latest.

checks.title: Do containers have security contexts configured (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, or allowPrivilegeEscalation=false)?
checks.evidence: 6/8 workload pods set a security context
checks.recommendation: Set a securityContext on every container (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false).

checks.title: Do containers run as non-root users?
checks.evidence: 11/14 workload containers run as non-root
checks.recommendation: Run containers as non-root (runAsNonRoot: true and a non-zero runAsUser).

checks.title: Are containers running without privileged mode?
checks.evidence: 14/14 workload containers are not privileged
checks.recommendation: Remove privileged: true from workload containers.

checks.title: Are pods free of host path volume mounts?
checks.evidence: 7/8 workload pods mount no hostPath volume; failing: legacy/log-shipper-x7k2p (hostPath /var/log)
checks.recommendation: Replace hostPath volumes with CSI or emptyDir volumes outside the system namespaces.

checks.title: Do containers add only the Linux capabilities the Pod Security Standards Baseline profile allows (no NET_ADMIN, SYS_ADMIN, SYS_MODULE, ALL)?
checks.evidence: 14/14 workload containers add no capability outside the Baseline set
checks.recommendation: Add only Baseline-allowed capabilities; drop NET_ADMIN, SYS_ADMIN and similar.

checks.title: Do containers drop ALL Linux capabilities?
checks.evidence: 6/14 workload containers drop ALL capabilities
checks.recommendation: Drop ALL capabilities and add back only what each container needs.

checks.title: Do EC2 worker nodes enforce IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required)?
checks.evidence: 6/6 running instances require IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required)
checks.recommendation: Require IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) on every node launch template or NodeClass.

checks.title: Do you implement container image signing and verification (Sigstore/Cosign, AWS Signer, Notary)?
checks.evidence: governance question: process only, not assessed from cluster data; confirm with the team
checks.recommendation: Sign images and verify signatures at admission.

checks.title: Is a runtime security monitoring agent present (GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring, Falco, Sysdig or Tetragon)?
checks.evidence: no GuardDuty add-on and no GuardDuty agent, Falco, Sysdig or Tetragon DaemonSet pods found
checks.recommendation: Run a runtime threat detection agent on every node (GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring or an equivalent).

checks.title: Do you use separate EKS clusters for production and non-production environments, ideally in different AWS accounts?
checks.evidence: governance question: process only, not assessed from cluster data; confirm with the team
checks.recommendation: Run production and non-production on separate clusters, ideally in separate accounts.

checks.title: Do you leverage tools like kube-bench to automatically check whether EKS is deployed securely by running checks documented in the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark?
checks.evidence: governance question: process only, not assessed from cluster data; confirm with the team
checks.recommendation: Run CIS benchmark checks (for example kube-bench) on a schedule.

checks.title: Do you manage configuration changes through version control with pull request reviews and approvals before applying to clusters?
checks.evidence: governance question: process only, not assessed from cluster data; confirm with the team
checks.recommendation: Change cluster configuration only through reviewed pull requests.

checks.title: Is Kubernetes audit logging enabled in the EKS control plane?
checks.evidence: control plane log type audit is enabled
checks.recommendation: Enable the audit control plane log type.

checks.title: Do you regularly scan your EKS cluster against compliance frameworks (CIS Benchmark, kube-bench)?
checks.evidence: governance question: process only, not assessed from cluster data; confirm with the team
checks.recommendation: Scan the cluster against a compliance framework on a schedule.

checks.title: Do you regularly scan your EKS cluster configuration against compliance frameworks (CIS Kubernetes Benchmark, PCI-DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2) using automated tools like kube-bench, Prowler, or AWS Security Hub?
checks.evidence: governance question: process only, not assessed from cluster data; confirm with the team
checks.recommendation: Automate configuration compliance scanning (kube-bench, Prowler or Security Hub).

checks.title: Do node instances block pod access to the instance metadata service (IMDSv2 required with hop limit 1, per node type)?
checks.evidence: 2/6 running Linux instances block pod access to IMDS (endpoint disabled, or IMDSv2 required with hop limit 1); failing: i-0bb1 (managed node group general, hop limit 2), i-0bb2 (managed node group general, hop limit 2), i-0bb3 (managed node group general, hop limit 2), i-0bb4 (managed node group general, hop limit 2)
checks.recommendation: Set HttpTokens=required and HttpPutResponseHopLimit=1 in each launch template, managed node group template or Karpenter EC2NodeClass; give pods that need AWS access Pod Identity or IRSA.

checks.title: Does every workload namespace carry a default-deny ingress NetworkPolicy?
checks.evidence: 2/4 workload namespaces carry a default-deny ingress NetworkPolicy (empty podSelector, Ingress, no ingress rule); objects only, enforcement is SEC-POSTURE-26 (WAR sec-4); failing: orders, web
checks.recommendation: Add a NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {} and policyTypes: [Ingress] to every workload namespace, then allow the flows each service needs.

checks.title: Is pod egress limited by a NetworkPolicy in every workload namespace?
checks.evidence: 0/4 workload namespaces limit egress for every pod (a NetworkPolicy with an empty podSelector and Egress in policyTypes); the allowed destinations are not judged; failing: orders, web, batch, legacy
checks.recommendation: Add a NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {} and policyTypes: [Egress] that allows DNS and the destinations each namespace needs.

checks.title: Are workload pods free of hostNetwork, hostPID and hostIPC outside the system namespaces?
checks.evidence: 7/8 workload pods use no host namespace; 1 pod(s) set hostNetwork, hostPID or hostIPC outside kube-* and amazon-*; failing: legacy/log-shipper-x7k2p (hostNetwork)
checks.recommendation: Remove hostNetwork, hostPID and hostIPC from workload pods; the Baseline Pod Security level rejects them.

checks.title: Is the control plane authenticator log enabled?
checks.evidence: control plane log types enabled: api, audit, authenticator; authenticator is on
checks.recommendation: Enable the authenticator control plane log type alongside audit (re-state every type already enabled).

checks.title: Is GuardDuty EKS Audit Log Monitoring enabled in this Region?
checks.evidence: not collected: guardduty.json (the read was denied or failed; see posture/meta.json errors), so this check was NOT measured
checks.recommendation: Enable GuardDuty and its EKS Audit Log Monitoring feature (EKS_AUDIT_LOGS) in this account and Region.

checks.title: Is GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring enabled for EKS in this Region?
checks.evidence: not collected: guardduty.json (the read was denied or failed; see posture/meta.json errors), so this check was NOT measured
checks.recommendation: Enable GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring with automated agent management for EKS (EKS_ADDON_MANAGEMENT).

checks.title: Is ECR registry scanning enhanced, with continuous rescan of every repository?
checks.evidence: registry scanType BASIC; rules: none; failing: scanType BASIC
checks.recommendation: Set registry scanning to ENHANCED with a CONTINUOUS_SCAN rule whose filter covers the repositories this cluster pulls (for example *).

checks.title: Are workload images referenced by immutable digest?
checks.evidence: 5/14 workload containers and init containers reference their image by @sha256: digest (the pod spec as written; a tag resolved at pull time does not count)
checks.recommendation: Reference images as repo@sha256:<digest> (CI can resolve tags to digests at deploy time).

checks.title: Is cluster-wide admin through an access policy held only by the expected principals (the roles named with --admin-allow)?
checks.evidence: 2 principal(s) hold cluster admin through an access policy outside --admin-allow (not given); the cluster was created with bootstrapClusterCreatorAdminPermissions true, so one of them is likely the creator; failing: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/platform-admin (AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy, cluster), arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/ci-deployer (AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy, cluster)
checks.recommendation: For each failing principal, grant what it needs at a narrower scope (AmazonEKSAdminPolicy with a namespace access scope, or a Kubernetes group bound to a narrower RBAC role), then remove the cluster-wide grant: aws eks disassociate-access-policy --cluster-name <CLUSTER> --region <REGION> --principal-arn <ARN> --policy-arn arn:aws:eks::aws:cluster-access-policy/<the listed policy, AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy or AmazonEKSAdminPolicy>. Keep one break-glass admin role whose use is logged. Printed for review; nothing is changed.
